sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Conventional Deadlift is one of the most fundamental compound exercises in strength training.

It involves lifting a loaded barbell from the ground to a standing position using a hip-width stance, engaging nearly every major muscle group in the body.

Often referred to as the king of all lifts, the conventional deadlift builds total body strength, power, and muscle mass like no other exercise.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.content:
- Builds total body strength and explosive power
- Develops the entire posterior chain (hamstrings, glutes, lower back)
- Improves grip strength and core stability
- Increases bone density and connective tissue strength
- Enhances athletic performance and functional strength
- Burns significant calories due to high muscle engagement
- Improves posture and spinal stability
- Carries over to real-world lifting mechanics

sections.heading: Muscles Worked
sections.content:
Primary: Erector Spinae, Glutes, Hamstrings, Quadriceps

Secondary: Trapezius, Latissimus Dorsi, Rhomboids, Core, Forearms and Grip, Calves

sections.heading: Starting Position
sections.content:
1. Stand with feet hip-width apart, barbell over mid-foot.
2. Barbell should be approximately 1 inch from your shins.
3. Bend at hips and knees to grip the bar.
4. Use an overhand grip (or mixed grip for heavier loads), hands just outside your legs.
5. Shoulders should be slightly in front of the bar.
6. Back should be neutral and flat, not rounded.
7. Chest up, shoulders down and back.
8. Eyes looking forward or slightly down.

sections.heading: Execution
sections.content:
1. Take a deep breath and brace your core tightly.
2. Pull the slack out of the bar before lifting.
3. Drive through your heels and mid-foot.
4. Extend your hips and knees simultaneously.
5. Keep the bar close to your body throughout the entire lift.
6. As the bar passes your knees, drive your hips forward.
7. Stand fully upright with shoulders back and hips locked out.
8. Reverse the movement to lower the bar with control.
9. Maintain a neutral spine throughout the entire movement.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Rounding the lower back (major injury risk)
- Starting with hips too high or too low
- Bar drifting away from the body
- Jerking or yanking the weight off the floor
- Not fully extending at the top (incomplete lockout)
- Looking up excessively and hyperextending the neck
- Dropping the bar on the way down without control
- Not bracing the core properly before each rep
- Using an improper grip width

sections.heading: Equipment Needed
sections.content:
- Olympic Barbell (45 lbs/20 kg)
- Weight Plates (bumper plates or iron plates)
- Lifting Platform or Suitable Floor Surface
- Optional: Lifting Belt (for heavy loads)
- Optional: Lifting Straps (for grip assistance)
- Optional: Chalk (improves grip)
- Recommended: Flat-soled shoes or deadlift slippers

sections.heading: Bar Setup
sections.content:
1. Load equal weight on both sides of the barbell.
2. Use collars to secure the plates.
3. Standard starting height with 45 lb plates is 9 inches off the ground.
4. For lighter weights, use blocks or rack pulls to maintain proper height.
5. Ensure the bar is on a flat, stable surface.
6. Bar should be straight and not bent.
7. Check that weights are secure before lifting.

sections.heading: Body Setup
sections.content:
1. Stance: Feet hip-width apart with a slight toe-out angle.
2. Bar Position: Over mid-foot (shoelaces area).
3. Grip: Just outside legs, arms straight and vertical.
4. Grip Options: Double overhand, mixed grip, or hook grip.
5. Hip Height: Should allow shoulders to be slightly over the bar.
6. Back Angle: Flat and neutral spine, never rounded.
7. Shoulder Position: Directly over or slightly in front of the bar.
8. Head Position: Neutral, in line with spine.

sections.heading: Similar Exercises
sections.content:
- Sumo Deadlift: Wide stance variation, more hip-dominant
- Trap Bar Deadlift: Easier on lower back, more quad emphasis
- Romanian Deadlift (RDL): Focuses on hamstrings and glutes
- Rack Pulls: Partial range deadlift from elevated position
- Deficit Deadlift: Standing on platform for increased range of motion
- Stiff-Leg Deadlift: Minimal knee bend, hamstring focus
- Snatch Grip Deadlift: Wide grip for increased upper back work

sections.heading: Deadlift Variations
sections.content:
Conventional Deadlift: Standard hip-width stance pull from floor
Sumo Deadlift: Wide stance, toes pointed out, more hip-dominant
Trap/Hex Bar Deadlift: Easier to learn, neutral grip position
Snatch Grip Deadlift: Wide grip, increased range of motion
Romanian Deadlift: Top-down movement, hamstring focus
Single-Leg Deadlift: Unilateral variation for balance and stability

sections.heading: If You Have Limitations
sections.content:
Lower Back Issues: Try trap bar deadlift or rack pulls
Grip Strength: Use lifting straps, chalk, or work on grip training
Mobility Issues: Start with rack pulls or Romanian deadlifts
No Barbell: Use dumbbells, kettlebells, or resistance bands
Form Concerns: Work with lighter weight and focus on technique
Hip Tightness: Consider sumo deadlift as an alternative
Learning Stage: Start with kettlebell deadlifts to master the hinge pattern
